topic: The Curious Link: Block Collisions and the Digits of Pi
target_audience: High school students interested in physics and mathematics

outline.topic: The Curious Link: Block Collisions and the Digits of Pi
outline.target_audience: High school students interested in physics and mathematics

sections.title: Introduction: The Impossible Counting Problem
sections.content: Introduce two blocks on a frictionless surface: a small block (mass m) and a large block (mass M). If M is a power of 100 (e.g., 100^n), the total number of elastic collisions between the blocks and a wall will exactly represent the first n+1 digits of Pi.
sections.example: Visualize two colorful robots (a small red cube and a giant blue block) colliding on a frictionless track; the blue block is massive, and the red one bounces back and forth like a ping-pong ball.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly review the conservation of momentum (mv1 + Mv2 = constant) and kinetic energy in perfectly elastic collisions. Explain that these laws create a mathematical mapping between the physical system and a geometric rotation.
sections.example: A 'collision diagram' showing a 2D space where the x and y axes represent the velocities of the two blocks. A collision is a reflection in this space.

sections.title: The Geometry of Collisions: The Phase Space
sections.content: Transform the collision problem into a geometric one. The state of the system traces a circular arc on a 2D plane. Each collision event corresponds to a reflection across a specific line determined by the mass ratio.
sections.example: An animation showing the velocity vector of the blocks rotating around a circle; every time the vector hits a 'boundary line', it signifies a physical collision.

sections.title: The Connection: Why Pi?
sections.content: Explain that the total angle covered by the rotation is proportional to Pi. As the mass M becomes infinitely large, the boundary lines force the 'bouncing' to count out the value of Pi in base-10 increments.
sections.example: A pie chart (pun intended) filling up piece by piece as the red block hits the blue block; each 'slice' added corresponds to a digit of 3.1415...

sections.title: Conclusion: Computation through Nature
sections.content: Summarize how a mechanical experiment acts as a digital computer. Emphasize that complex mathematical constants like Pi are embedded in the fundamental laws of motion.
sections.example: Final screen showing: 1 collision = '3', 14 more = '1', 159 more = '4'... a 'Mechanical Pi Calculator'.

storyboard.title: Introduction: The Impossible Counting Problem
lecture_lines: Two blocks collide on a frictionless surface.
The small block hits the large block repeatedly.
Total collisions reveal the digits of Pi.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
lecture_lines: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy.
These laws map physical states to geometric rotations.
Collisions behave like reflections in a velocity plane.
animations: Display energy conservation formula E_initial = E_final #FFFF00
Animate energy bar shifting from one state to another #00FFFF

storyboard.title: The Geometry of Collisions: The Phase Space
lecture_lines: Collision dynamics trace a circular arc.
Each boundary hit reflects the movement path.
Geometry encodes the system's ongoing state changes.
animations: Display title #FFFFFF: 'The Geometry of Collisions: The Phase Space'
Draw a 2D plane with two axes showing velocity components #FFFFFF
Show a path representing elastic collision trajectory in phase space #FF00FF

storyboard.title: The Connection: Why Pi?
lecture_lines: The rotation angle is proportional to Pi.
Massive blocks force the path to subdivide.
Subdivisions precisely count the decimal digits of Pi.
animations: Overlay a circular arc on the collision trajectory path #FFFF00
Display the emergence of PI within the collision count #FFFFFF

storyboard.title: Conclusion: Computation through Nature
lecture_lines: Nature acts as a mechanical Pi calculator.
Physical motion maps to abstract mathematical constants.
We see Pi through these mechanical collisions.
animations: Fade in a digital calculator vs natural collision system #00FF00
Flash final result with highlight #FFFFFF: 'Nature Computes'
